p: Long ago, a king called Lir had four children: a daughter, Fionnuala, and three sons. Their mother died, and Lir married her sister, Aoife. At first she was kind, but she soon became jealous of the love between Lir and his children.

One day she took the children to a lake and used a magic spell to turn them into swans. The spell would last nine hundred years. The swans kept their human voices, and their beautiful singing brought comfort to everyone who heard it.

When the spell finally ended, the swans became people again, but they were now very old. Before they died, a kind monk baptised them. Today you can see a statue of the four swans in the Garden of Remembrance in Dublin.
An old poet called Finnegas spent seven years beside the River Boyne, trying to catch a special salmon. People believed that the first person to eat this fish would know everything in the world.

At last he caught it and asked his young helper, Fionn, to cook it, but warned him not to taste it. While the fish was cooking, Fionn touched the hot skin and burned his thumb. Without thinking, he put his thumb in his mouth.

When Finnegas saw the boy's face, he understood immediately: Fionn had received all the knowledge of the salmon. From that day, whenever Fionn needed wisdom, he simply sucked his thumb. He later became the famous leader of the Fianna warriors.

t.ja: ジャイアンツ・コーズウェー

p: On the north coast of Ireland, about forty thousand stone columns stand side by side like stepping stones going into the sea. Scientists say they were formed by cooling lava millions of years ago, but the legend is much more exciting.

The story says that the Irish giant Fionn built a path across the sea to fight a Scottish giant called Benandonner. When Fionn saw how huge his enemy was, he ran home in fear. His clever wife dressed him as a baby and put him in a cradle.

When Benandonner arrived and saw the enormous baby, he thought: if the child is this big, the father must be gigantic. He ran back to Scotland, breaking the path behind him so that nobody could follow.

t.en: Oisín and the Land of Youth
t.es: Oisín y la Tierra de la Juventud

p: Oisín, the son of Fionn, was a great warrior and poet. One day a beautiful woman called Niamh rode out of the sea on a white horse and invited him to Tír na nÓg, the Land of Youth, where nobody ever grows old.

Oisín went with her, and they lived there happily. After what felt like three years, he missed his family and asked to visit Ireland. Niamh lent him her horse but warned him never to touch the ground.

In Ireland everything had changed. Three hundred years had passed, and his friends were long gone. When he bent down from the horse to help some men lift a stone, he fell to the ground and instantly became a very old man.

t.en: How Cú Chulainn Got His Name
t.hi: कू खुलैन को नाम कैसे मिला
t.es: Cómo recibió su nombre Cú Chulainn
t.ja: クー・フーリンの名前の由来

p: Cú Chulainn is the greatest hero of old Irish stories, but as a boy his name was Sétanta. One evening the king was invited to a feast at the house of Culann, a blacksmith who kept a fierce guard dog.
Sétanta was playing hurling and arrived late. Nobody remembered that he was still outside, so the hound was released. When the dog ran at him, the boy hit his ball so hard that it killed the animal.

Culann was sad, because the dog had protected his home. Sétanta promised to train a new puppy and, until it was ready, to guard the house himself. From then on people called him Cú Chulainn, which means the Hound of Culann.
In Irish folklore, the banshee is a female spirit whose cry warns a family that someone is going to die. The name comes from the Irish words bean sí, which mean woman of the fairy mounds.

Some people describe her as a young and beautiful woman, while others say she is an old woman with long grey hair and red eyes from crying. She is often seen near rivers, combing her hair with a silver comb.

Traditionally, the banshee only followed certain old Irish families. She was not thought to be evil; she simply mourned for the dead. For this reason, many children were told never to pick up a comb they found lying on the ground.

The leprechaun is probably the most famous fairy in Ireland. In old stories he is a small, grumpy shoemaker who works alone, and you can sometimes find him by listening for the tapping of his tiny hammer.
Leprechauns are said to hide pots of gold. If you catch one, he must lead you to his treasure, but you must not take your eyes off him for even a second. If you look away, he will disappear.

In one tale, a farmer caught a leprechaun, who showed him the bush where the gold was buried. The farmer tied a red ribbon to the bush and went home for a spade. When he returned, every bush in the field had a red ribbon.

t.ja: 聖ブリジッドのマント

p: Saint Brigid is one of Ireland's patron saints, and since 2023 her feast day on the first of February has been a public holiday. She is said to have founded a famous convent in Kildare around the year 480.

According to legend, Brigid asked the King of Leinster for land to build her convent. The king laughed and said she could have as much land as her cloak could cover. She smiled and spread her cloak on the ground.

Suddenly the cloak began to grow, spreading in every direction until it covered many acres. The surprised king kept his promise. Even today, people make Saint Brigid's crosses from rushes and hang them in their homes for protection.
The Cliffs of Moher stretch for about fourteen kilometres along the coast of County Clare. At their highest point they rise more than two hundred metres above the wild Atlantic Ocean.

They are one of the most visited natural attractions in Ireland, welcoming well over a million visitors every year. On a clear day you can see the Aran Islands and the hills of Connemara from the top.

The cliffs are also an important home for seabirds. In spring and summer thousands of puffins, razorbills and guillemots nest on the narrow ledges. Visitors are asked to stay behind the safety walls, because the edge can be dangerous in strong winds.

The Burren in County Clare looks like a grey moon landscape. Its name comes from the Irish word boireann, meaning a rocky place. Huge flat areas of limestone are cut by deep cracks that the rain has made over thousands of years.
Although the land looks empty, it is full of life. Flowers from the Arctic, the Alps and the Mediterranean all grow here side by side, which surprises scientists from around the world.

The Burren is also rich in history. More than ninety ancient tombs can be found there, including the Poulnabrone dolmen, a huge stone table that is over five thousand years old. Farmers still bring their cattle up to the hills to graze in winter.

t.ja: スケリッグ・マイケル

p: Skellig Michael is a steep, rocky island about twelve kilometres off the coast of County Kerry. Over a thousand years ago, a small group of monks chose to live there, far away from the rest of the world.

They built stone huts shaped like beehives and carved more than six hundred steps into the rock. Life was extremely hard: they caught fish, kept a small garden and collected rainwater, while storms battered the island for much of the year.

Today the island is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and home to thousands of puffins. It became even more famous after scenes from the Star Wars films were shot there. Boats can only land when the sea is calm.

Newgrange in County Meath was built around 3200 BC, which makes it older than Stonehenge and the Great Pyramids of Egypt. It is a large round mound with a long stone passage leading to a chamber inside.

The most amazing thing about Newgrange happens at the winter solstice. For a few days around the twenty-first of December, the rising sun shines through a small opening above the entrance and lights up the inner chamber for about seventeen minutes.

Every year thousands of people enter a lottery for the chance to stand inside the tomb on those special mornings. The builders had no metal tools, yet they lined up the passage with the sun almost perfectly.

Glendalough, which means the valley of the two lakes, lies in the Wicklow Mountains, about an hour's drive south of Dublin. In the sixth century a monk called Saint Kevin came here to live a quiet life alone.

Many followers joined him, and a large monastic settlement slowly grew up in the valley. You can still see its stone churches and a round tower about thirty metres tall, which was used as a bell tower and a lookout.

A popular story says that Kevin once stood with his arms open in prayer for so long that a blackbird built a nest in his hand. He waited without moving until the eggs hatched. Today walkers enjoy the forest paths around both lakes.
The Aran Islands lie at the mouth of Galway Bay. There are three of them: Inis Mór, Inis Meáin and Inis Oírr. Irish is still the everyday language for many of the people who live there.

The islands are covered in a huge network of dry stone walls, built by hand over hundreds of years to clear the rocky fields. Farmers made soil by mixing sand with seaweed so that they could grow potatoes.

On Inis Mór stands Dún Aonghasa, an ancient stone fort on the edge of a cliff high above the ocean. The islands are also famous for the thick Aran sweater, whose patterns were traditionally passed down through families.

t.en: Galway, the City of the Tribes
t.es: Galway, la ciudad de las tribus
t.ja: 部族の街ゴールウェイ

p: Galway is a lively city on the west coast of Ireland. It is often called the City of the Tribes because, in the Middle Ages, fourteen powerful merchant families controlled its trade and politics.

Ships from Spain and France once sailed into its harbour carrying wine and salt. Near the river you can still see the Spanish Arch, part of the old city walls. Today the narrow streets are full of musicians, cafés and small shops.

Every July the city hosts the Galway International Arts Festival, which attracts visitors from all over the world. Galway is also the home of the Claddagh ring, a traditional Irish ring showing two hands holding a crowned heart.

Dingle is a colourful fishing town in County Kerry, at the far western edge of Europe. It is part of the Gaeltacht, an area where Irish is spoken in daily life, so many signs are written only in Irish.
For almost forty years, from 1983, a wild dolphin called Fungie lived in Dingle harbour. He loved to swim beside boats, and he became the town's most famous resident until he disappeared in 2020.
The nearby Slea Head Drive is one of the most beautiful roads in Ireland. It passes ancient stone huts, sandy beaches and views of the Blasket Islands, whose last residents left the islands in 1953.

t.ja: 大理石の街キルケニー

p: Kilkenny is a small city in the south-east of Ireland with a strong medieval character. It is known as the Marble City because of the dark local limestone, which shines like black marble when it is polished.

A walking route called the Medieval Mile links the main sights, from the grand Kilkenny Castle to the beautiful Saint Canice's Cathedral, where you can climb a round tower for a view over the rooftops.

Kilkenny is also famous for its creative spirit. Every August a large arts festival fills the streets, and the Kilkenny Design Centre has supported Irish craftspeople since the 1960s. Many visitors finish their day in one of the city's traditional pubs.

Connemara is a wild region in the west of County Galway, famous for its mountains, lakes and empty bogs. The light changes quickly here, and painters and photographers have loved the landscape for centuries.

The Twelve Bens, a group of sharp mountains, rise above the area, while hundreds of small lakes reflect the sky. In the past, families cut turf from the bogs, dried it in the sun and burned it to heat their homes.

Connemara also gives its name to a strong, gentle breed of pony that has lived in the area for a very long time. Kylemore Abbey, a castle beside a lake that later became a home for nuns, is one of the most photographed buildings in Ireland.

Saint Patrick is the most famous patron saint of Ireland, but he was not Irish. He was born in Roman Britain in the fifth century. When he was about sixteen, raiders kidnapped him and brought him to Ireland as a slave.
For six years he looked after sheep on a lonely hillside, and during this hard time he became deeply religious. Finally he escaped, made his way home and later studied to become a priest.

Years afterwards he returned to Ireland to spread Christianity. Legend says that he used the three leaves of the shamrock to explain the Holy Trinity. Today people all over the world celebrate Saint Patrick's Day on the seventeenth of March with parades and green clothes.

The Book of Kells is a beautifully decorated copy of the four Gospels, made by monks around the year 800. Many experts believe it was started on the Scottish island of Iona and finished at the monastery of Kells in County Meath.

Its pages are made of calfskin, and the colours came from plants, minerals and even insects. The pictures are full of tiny details: knots, spirals, animals and faces that are hard to see without a magnifying glass.

During its long history the book was stolen and its golden cover was lost, but the pages survived. Since the seventeenth century it has been kept at Trinity College Dublin, where hundreds of thousands of visitors come to see it every year.
Brian Boru is one of the best-known kings in Irish history. He was born in County Clare around the year 941 and rose from being a local prince to become High King of Ireland.
Brian was a strong leader who united many of the Irish kingdoms for the first time. He also supported monasteries and schools, and he was proud to call himself Emperor of the Irish.

In 1014 he led his army against the King of Leinster and his Viking allies at the Battle of Clontarf, near Dublin. Brian's side won the battle, but the old king was killed in his tent. The harp on Irish coins is often linked to his name.

t.ja: ヴァイキングとダブリン

p: The Vikings first raided Ireland at the end of the eighth century, attacking rich monasteries along the coast. Later, instead of simply raiding, they began to build permanent settlements.

In the ninth century they set up a base beside a dark pool where the River Poddle met the River Liffey. The Irish name for it was Dubh Linn, meaning black pool, and this is where the name Dublin comes from.

The Vikings turned Dublin into a busy trading town. They also founded other towns such as Wexford, Waterford and Limerick. Over time they married into Irish families, and archaeologists have found thousands of their objects under the streets of the modern city.
In the 1840s, many poor families in Ireland depended almost completely on the potato for food. In 1845 a plant disease called blight arrived, and the potatoes rotted in the fields.

The disease returned in the following years, and the result was a terrible famine that lasted until about 1852. Around one million people died from hunger and illness, while food was still being exported from the country.

More than a million others left Ireland on crowded ships, often called coffin ships, to start new lives in America, Canada, Britain and Australia. The famine changed Ireland forever, and memorials to its victims stand in Dublin and in cities across the world.

t.ja: タイタニック号とアイルランド

p: The Titanic was built in Belfast by the shipbuilders Harland and Wolff. Thousands of workers spent about three years building it, and when it was launched in 1911 it was the largest moving object ever made.

In April 1912 the ship left Southampton on its first voyage. Its last stop before crossing the Atlantic was Queenstown in County Cork, now called Cobh, where more than a hundred passengers came on board.

Just four days later the Titanic hit an iceberg and sank, and around fifteen hundred people lost their lives. Today Titanic Belfast, a museum shaped like the bows of a ship, stands close to the place where it was built.

Irish, or Gaeilge, is one of the oldest written languages in Europe. It is the first official language of Ireland, and every child learns it at school, even though English is the language most people use every day.

After the Great Famine, the number of Irish speakers fell sharply, as many families saw English as the key to a better future. Areas where Irish is still the main community language are called the Gaeltacht.

Today Irish is enjoying a quiet revival. There is a national Irish-language television channel, and road signs show place names in both languages. You will also hear Irish words in everyday English in Ireland, such as craic, which means fun.

t.ja: 最初のハロウィン、サウィン

p: Halloween began in Ireland more than two thousand years ago as Samhain, an ancient festival that marked the end of the harvest and the start of the dark half of the year.

People believed that on this night the wall between our world and the world of spirits became thin. To protect themselves, they lit huge bonfires and wore disguises so that the spirits would not recognise them.

When Irish emigrants travelled to America in the nineteenth century, they took their customs with them. In Ireland people had carved scary faces into turnips, but in America they found that pumpkins were bigger and much easier to carve.
